title: Privacy Policy
body:
This notice explains what personal data LangNation collects, why, how long we keep it and what rights you have. It follows the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and German data protection law.

In short. We collect only what we need to teach you and to answer you. We do not sell your data, we do not use advertising trackers, and our analytics counts page views without identifying anyone. You can ask us at any time what we hold, and ask us to correct or delete it.

1. Who is responsible

The controller for the processing described here is the organisation named in our Imprint, which also gives our postal address and contact details. Write to us there about anything on this page.

2. What we collect, and why

When you send an enquiry

The contact form asks for your name, email address and message, and optionally your phone number, country and the course you are interested in. We also record the page you sent it from and your IP address.

  • Why: to answer you, and to recognise automated submissions.
  • Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR — steps taken at your request before entering a contract; and Art. 6(1)(f) — our legitimate interest in keeping the form usable.
  • Kept: up to two years after our last exchange, then deleted.

When you ask for a portal account

We ask for your name, email address and your reason for wanting an account, and optionally your phone number and country.

  • Why: so a person can decide whether to grant the account, and tell you either way.
  • Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR.
  • Kept: approved requests for as long as the account exists; declined ones for up to twelve months, so a decision can be reviewed or reversed.

When you hold a portal account

Your name, email address, contact details, course enrolments, attendance, placement test results and any certificates issued.

  • Why: to provide the course and the portal.
  • Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR.
  • Kept: while you are a student and afterwards only as long as the law requires — commercial and tax records must be kept for six or ten years under §257 HGB and §147 AO.

When you take the placement test

Your answers and the resulting level.

  • Why: to recommend the right course.
  • Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR.
  • Kept: twelve months, or for as long as you hold an account.

When you simply read the site

Our server records the page requested, the time and the language. We count page views to see which pages are useful.

  • Why: to keep the site working and to improve it.
  • Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR — our legitimate interest in a functioning website.
  • Kept: counts are aggregated and hold nothing that identifies a person.

We use no Google Analytics, no advertising pixels and no cross-site tracking of any kind.

3. Cookies

We set cookies only where they are needed for something you asked for:

  • Session cookie — keeps you signed in to the student portal. Deleted when the session ends.
  • Theme preference — remembers whether you chose light or dark. Stored in your browser, never sent to us.

These are strictly necessary, so no consent banner is required for them under §25(2) TTDSG. We set no advertising or analytics cookies.

4. Who else sees your data

Only those who must, and only to do their part:

  • Our hosting provider, which runs the servers and the mail service, under a data processing agreement (Art. 28 GDPR).
  • Examination bodies such as telc or the Goethe-Institut, where you ask us to register you for an examination.
  • Public authorities, where the law requires it.

We do not sell personal data and do not pass it to advertisers.

5. Transfers outside the EU

Our servers are in the European Union. Where a service we use processes data outside the EU, we rely on an adequacy decision of the European Commission or on Standard Contractual Clauses.

6. Machine translation

The German pages of this site were prepared with the help of DeepL, a translation service operated in Germany. Page content was sent for translation; no personal data of yours was involved.

7. Your rights

Under the GDPR you may ask us to:

  • tell you what we hold about you, and give you a copy (Art. 15);
  • correct anything inaccurate (Art. 16);
  • delete your data, where no legal duty requires us to keep it (Art. 17);
  • restrict how we use it (Art. 18);
  • hand it over in a portable form (Art. 20);
  • object to processing based on our legitimate interest (Art. 21);
  • withdraw consent at any time, where processing rests on consent (Art. 7(3)). This does not affect what was lawful before.

Write to the address in our Imprint. We answer within one month.

8. Complaints

If you think we have handled your data wrongly, please tell us first — most things are a misunderstanding we can fix quickly.

You also have the right to complain to a supervisory authority, in the EU state where you live, work, or where the issue arose. In Germany this is the data protection authority of the federal state in which we are established.

9. Is giving us data required?

Only where it is needed. We cannot teach you a course without your name and a way to reach you. Everything marked optional on a form really is optional, and leaving it blank changes nothing about how we treat you.

10. Automated decisions

We make no automated decisions producing legal effects concerning you, and we do not profile you.

Submissions to our forms are scored automatically for signs of automated abuse. A submission that scores highly is set aside for a person to look at rather than acted on by the machine, and no account or enrolment decision is ever made this way.

11. Changes to this notice

We update this page when what we do changes. The version in force is the one published here.

ECTS is the abbreviation of the European Credit Transfer and accumulation System. It is an academic credit system that performs on the basis of the required students’ workload. It helps to achieve the objectives and learning outcomes. ECTS works for a module or program of study.

The structure of ECTS is designed by keeping the academic recognition for the period of study in mind. The purpose is to facilitate students’ mobility and credit accumulation and transfer as well. If the student is moving across Europe for higher education, the ECTS credit system comes as a savior.

title: The German school system
body:
Germany does not have one school system. Education is a matter for the sixteen federal states rather than the federal government, so it has sixteen of them — alike in shape, different in almost every detail. The diagram above is the shape. This page is what it means, and where each line on it leads.

Kindergarten

Children may attend a Kindergarten or Kita from the age of three. It is not compulsory and it is not school: there are no grades, no marks and no report. Since 2013 every child has had a legal entitlement to a place in early-years care from their first birthday, although in the larger cities demand runs well ahead of supply and a place is worth applying for long before you need it.

For a family arriving from abroad this is usually where a child’s German begins, and it is the reason children who arrive before school age tend to walk into their first classroom already speaking.

Grundschule: the part everybody does

School becomes compulsory at six. It begins with the Grundschule, which runs from grade 1 to grade 4 across most of Germany and to grade 6 in Berlin and Brandenburg. Every child attends the same kind of school, studies broadly the same subjects and is taught for most of the week by one class teacher.

What makes the Grundschule weigh more than a primary school elsewhere is not what happens inside it but what happens at the end of it.

The branch at the end of Grundschule

At the end of grade 4 — or grade 6 — children move on to one of several kinds of secondary school. The Grundschule issues a recommendation based on the child’s marks and how they have worked. In some states that recommendation is binding; in others the parents decide and the school only advises.

It is the most consequential moment in a German school career, and it arrives when the child is ten. Several states soften it with an Orientierungsstufe, an observation phase covering grades 5 and 6 during which moving to a different school is still straightforward.

Hauptschule

Grades 5 to 9, ending in the Hauptschulabschluss. The same subjects as everywhere else, taught at a gentler pace and with a steadier eye on practical work. It leads most directly into an Ausbildung, and a pupil who does well can go on to the mittlere Reife afterwards rather than instead.

Realschule

Grades 5 to 10, ending in the mittlere Reife. The broad middle of the system, and the usual route into the commercial and technical apprenticeships. A strong leaving certificate opens the Fachoberschule, and in most states a strong enough one opens the Gymnasium itself.

Gesamtschule

A comprehensive school holding all of the above under one roof, so that every leaving qualification stays reachable and the decision at ten is not final. Where a state offers one it is often the answer for a family that does not yet know how a child will settle — which describes most families who have just moved country.

Gymnasium

Grades 5 to 12 or 13, ending in the Abitur. The academic route, a second and often third foreign language, and the only school type that carries a pupil all the way to a university entrance qualification without changing school.

What comes after school

Berufsausbildung

The dual apprenticeship: two to three and a half years split between a company that pays a training wage and a Berufsschule that teaches the theory. It ends in a nationally recognised qualification and it is not a second-best route — a large part of German industry is staffed and led by people who came through it.

Fachoberschule, and the Fachhochschulreife

Two years after the mittlere Reife, ending in the Fachhochschulreife: an entrance qualification for a Fachhochschule, the universities of applied sciences. It is the standard second chance for anyone who left school at 16 and later decided they wanted to study.

The Oberstufe and the Abitur

The last two or three years of the Gymnasium, also available at a Berufliches Gymnasium alongside a vocational specialism. It ends in the Abitur — the allgemeine Hochschulreife — which qualifies the holder for any German university and any subject, subject to the entry restrictions individual courses impose.

Whether the Abitur comes at the end of grade 12 or grade 13 depends on the state, and several have changed their minds about it twice.

University

The Fachhochschulreife opens the Fachhochschulen. The Abitur opens those and the universities. Tuition at public universities is free or close to it for German and international students alike in most states, with a semester contribution of a few hundred euros that usually includes a local transport ticket.

Nothing here is the same in every state

Every figure on this page has an exception somewhere. Grundschule is six years in two states. Hauptschule and Realschule have been merged into a single school type in several others, under a different name in each. The recommendation at the end of grade 4 binds parents in some states and advises them in the rest.

So use this page and the diagram for the shape of the thing, and check the detail with the school authority of the state you are actually moving to.

Where German comes into it

Every route on this page is taught in German. Schools in most states run preparatory or welcome classes for children arriving without it, and an Ausbildung or a degree course will normally ask for B1 or B2 before it will take you. That is the practical reason the language comes first, and it is the part we can help with.

title: Grundschule
body:
The Grundschule is the primary school every German child attends, and the only stage of the system where they all attend the same kind of school. It runs from grade 1 to grade 4 — to grade 6 in Berlin and Brandenburg — and it ends with the decision that shapes everything after it.

Starting school

School is compulsory from six, with the exact cut-off date set by each state. Children are normally assigned to the Grundschule for the district they live in rather than choosing one, which is worth knowing before you sign a tenancy agreement: in Germany the flat you take decides the school you get.

The first day is called the Einschulung and it is a genuine occasion — a ceremony at the school, the family there, and the Schultüte, a large decorated cone of sweets and small presents that the child carries in. If you have just arrived, take the camera. Everyone else will have.

The school day

A traditional Grundschule day ends around lunchtime, which comes as a shock to parents used to a full working day of school. That is changing: Ganztagsschulen running into the afternoon are now common and expanding, and where the school itself finishes early a Hort provides supervised care afterwards. Both usually need to be applied for, and both can have waiting lists.

What is taught

German, mathematics, and a general subject variously called Sachunterricht that covers science, history, geography and civics together. Art, music and sport throughout. A first foreign language, almost always English, begins in grade 1 or grade 3 depending on the state. Religion or ethics is timetabled, and which of the two a child takes is the family’s choice.

Marks usually do not appear until grade 3. Before that, reports are written in sentences.

Children arriving without German

A child who arrives in Germany without the language is not held back a year for it. Most states run preparatory classes — Willkommensklasse, Vorbereitungsklasse, DaZ-Klasse, the name changes with the state — where the child is taught German intensively while joining the ordinary class for sport, art and music, and moves across fully as the language comes.

Primary-age children reach fluency remarkably fast, and it is common for the child to be translating for the parents inside a year. The parents are the ones who tend to need the course.

The recommendation at the end

In the final year the school issues a recommendation for the kind of secondary school it believes suits the child: Hauptschule, Realschule, Gesamtschule or Gymnasium. It rests on marks, but also on how the child works — independence, concentration, how they handle being stuck.

In some states the recommendation binds; in others it advises and the parents decide. Either way it is worth talking to the class teacher early rather than meeting the recommendation for the first time on paper, and worth knowing that it is not as final as it feels. Children move between school types afterwards, and the routes described in the overview of the system exist precisely so that a decision made at ten can be revisited at sixteen.

title: Realschule
body:
The Realschule covers grades 5 to 10 and ends in the mittlere Reife. It is the broad middle of the German system: more academic than the Hauptschule, more practical than the Gymnasium, and the usual route into the apprenticeships that need a solid general education first.

What it leads to

The leaving qualification is the Mittlerer Schulabschluss, almost always called the mittlere Reife. It is the entry requirement for a large share of German apprenticeships — commercial, technical, administrative and medical — and for much of the public sector’s intermediate grades.

It is also a door rather than a ceiling. With it a pupil can go on to a Fachoberschule for two years and gain the Fachhochschulreife, and from there to a university of applied sciences. In most states a strong enough mittlere Reife also allows a transfer into the Oberstufe of a Gymnasium and on to the Abitur.

What is taught

German, mathematics, English, the sciences, history, geography and civics, with a second foreign language usually available as an option from grade 6 or 7 — commonly French, Spanish or Latin. Most Realschulen build in subject strands from around grade 7 so a pupil can lean towards languages, science or the economic and technical subjects.

Work experience is part of the course rather than an extra. A Praktikum of one to three weeks, often in grade 8 or 9, is standard, and it is frequently how a pupil finds the firm that later takes them on.

It is not called Realschule everywhere

Several states have merged the Hauptschule and the Realschule into a single secondary school offering both leaving qualifications, and each has given it a different name: Oberschule, Mittelschule, Sekundarschule, Stadtteilschule, Realschule plus, Gemeinschaftsschule. The qualification at the end is the same recognised mittlere Reife.

So if the state you are moving to appears to have no Realschule, it almost certainly has the thing itself under another name. The school authority for the state will tell you which.

Arriving from another country

Foreign school reports are assessed for equivalence by the state authority, and a pupil is usually placed by age and by the level demonstrated rather than by the certificate alone. Where German is the obstacle rather than the ability, the preparatory classes described on the Grundschule page continue at secondary level, and the pupil moves into the ordinary timetable subject by subject.

The realistic requirement is that the German comes first: the subjects are taught in it, and the leaving examination is written in it. The overview of the system sets out where the mittlere Reife sits and what it opens.

title: Gymnasium
body:
The Gymnasium is the academic route through German secondary education. It runs from grade 5 to grade 12 or 13 and ends in the Abitur, the qualification that opens every German university and, in principle, every subject in them.

Eight years or nine

Whether the Abitur comes at the end of grade 12 or grade 13 depends on the state, and this is the part of the German system that has changed most in living memory. Most states shortened the Gymnasium from nine years to eight in the 2000s; a number have since moved back, or now offer both and let the family choose. Check the state, not the country.

What is taught

The full academic range: German, mathematics, English, physics, chemistry, biology, geography, history, civics, computer science, art, music and sport, with philosophy or ethics alongside religion. A second foreign language is compulsory, normally from grade 6 — French, Latin or Spanish most often — and a third is usually available as an option.

The last two or three years are the gymnasiale Oberstufe, where the class timetable gives way to a system of courses at basic and advanced level. Pupils choose advanced subjects, and those choices, together with the final examinations, produce the Abitur grade.

The Abitur

The Abitur is the allgemeine Hochschulreife — the general higher education entrance qualification. The final mark combines the results of the last two years with the leaving examinations, so it is an assessment of a period rather than of one week, and it is expressed on a scale where 1.0 is the best attainable.

It qualifies the holder for any German university. It does not by itself guarantee a place on any particular course: popular subjects restrict entry by grade, and medicine in particular is competitive by a distance.

The same qualification by another route

A Berufliches Gymnasium teaches the same Oberstufe alongside a vocational specialism — business, engineering, health, social care — and awards the same Abitur. It is usually entered after the mittlere Reife rather than at grade 5, which makes it one of the main ways into a university for somebody who did not go to a Gymnasium at ten.

That is worth saying plainly, because the branch at the end of the Grundschule looks more final than it is: the routes are set out in the overview of the system, and several of them end at the same place.

Arriving from another country

Entry depends on the state authority’s assessment of the school record so far, and on German. The Gymnasium teaches demanding subject matter in German to native speakers, so a pupil arriving without the language is normally placed in a preparatory class first and moves across subject by subject.

For anyone planning the university route from abroad, the German is not a formality to be dealt with later. It is the entry requirement to the school that awards the qualification.

title: Master
body:
Masters study program in Germany

Many students prefer Germany for their postgraduation study across the globe. The entire credit goes to the strong economy of the place with a rich historical background. Germany offers a large number of English courses to students worldwide.
The top-ranked universities of Germany are attracting students. This throng of students is much greater than other universities in the USA and UK. Here, the exemption of tuition fees is another compelling reason.
Here is the guide to creating better comprehension of Masters Study in Germany. A student collects many questions before approaching admission, from the student Visa to the German university system works. This guide can answer those questions in the best possible way.
Masters’ / Postgraduate opportunities in Germany
Germany is indeed a blessed land with ideas and history. The land has an indelible association with some of history’s most formidable thinkers. Immanuel Kant, Albert Einstein, and Werner Heisenberg like renowned names are the real gems of this ‘land of ideas’.

Here are a few compelling reasons to choose Germany over many other locations –
  • Germany has a rich historical background that derives ingenuity and innovation. The enlightenment and the industrial revolution are the two big reasons behind the development of Germany. Arts, theology, and philosophy contribute to the learning system development of German in various terms like engineering and science.
  • Academic freedom, integrity, and rigor of German universities have gone through the inventions. The German thinkers like Wilhelm von Humboldt are responsible people for the development in the 19th century.
  • Germany offers a generous post-study work opportunity to the students. The EU and non-EU graduates are getting better explosion to the place. It has around 13% of students who have come here from other locations.
  • Top-ranked German universities are providing world-renowned qualifications.
  • The cost of living is quite moderate in Germany compared to other European countries. On the other hand, many German universities don’t even charge tuition fees.

German Universities

With around 400 universities and 20,000-degree programs, Germany is leading the academics. You must explore well before choosing one!
Get a sense of opinion:
Types of German Universities

Four types of German Universities are here –
  1. Research Universities (Universität): It carries out the original academic work of various subjects like research. They offer Masters and Ph.D. degrees.
  2. Technical Universities (Technische Universität): Such universities are owning the expertise in science, technology, and engineering research. There are many more qualifications that these universities offer.
  3. Universities of Applied Science (Fachhochschulen): These universities focus on engineering, business, or a social science like practical subjects. These universities are partnered with different organizations and professionals.
  4. Colleges of Art, Film, and Music: These colleges are specialized in practical instruction with creative disciplines. If a student seeks admission in such colleges, they need to demonstrate creative skills
The renowned research institutes of Germany are performing important research projects. Max Planck Society runs these institutes and the associated projects. Everything is performed under the partnership with the industry, universities, and businesses. These institutes offer Ph.D. level qualification, not below that.
Private vs Public Universities
16 states (or lander) are there in Germany where each one carries the responsibility of administering the public universities. The state funding and fees of these universities can be handled at the state level educational system.
Around 300 public universities are floating in Germany. A large number of students are enrolled here that can even reach up to 95%, as per the estimation of the DAAD (the official German Academic Exchange Service). 
On the other hand, around 120 institutions are private universities. These universities are free to plan their tuition fees and they don’t receive state funding. This can also give them an exemption to charge more fees than public universities.
Public and private universities offer great opportunities to the students where they can develop their careers well. The only difference between these two streams is the fee they charge.

German University cities

German is the ultimate place that welcomes everyone. The student-friendly cities give a warm welcome to education seekers. Berlin and Heidelberg like cities render the amazes that can attract the students enormously. The perfection of the place is awesome and the relaxed atmosphere is indeed suitable for the students. 

Some main universities of cities and towns are listed here –
  • Berlin 
  • Munich
  • Nuremberg
  • Hamburg
  • Cologne
  • Frankfurt am Mein
  • Stuttgart

German Masters Degrees

Course Length & Credit Value
The usual duration of German Masters's programs is two-year (approx two to four semesters). The complete degree is worth 120 ECTS credits. These 120 ECTS credits can be classified into two main parts. The modules, exams, and coursework offer 90 ECTS credits whereas the dissertation offers 30 ECTS credits. 
Degree Types
German Masters degrees award MA (Master of Arts) or MSc (Master of Science) qualifications. The specialized subjects are also providing alternative degrees. The variation in learning and study creates the main differentiation between the programs. The German Master's degrees are classified into two ways, consecutive and non-consecutive.

  1. Consecutive Masters Degrees: These programs don’t charge a fee. Students might study for a Masters's program after Graduation in a similar stream. Thus, these degrees follow the close related undergraduate degree.
  2. Non-consecutive Masters Degrees: These courses are more professional and practical in comparison to other streams. This also charges fees and focuses on a different as well as highly specialized area.
The German Master's degrees require appropriate consecutive Bachelor's degree programs.

Course Content 

There are separate learning modules for German Masters degrees. This content gets different as per the program. It depends on the selection of students where he or she prefers practical workshops, fieldwork, small-group seminars, lectures, or independent study.
Research University includes different seminars and lectures, practical works, reading and independent study, etc. The practical works are performed in the laboratory. On the other hand, the University of Applied Science includes more hands-on training that lacks in the previous one. It further focuses on workshops, organized by external and industry experts. College of Art, Film, and Music include artistic programs with all the practical skills and proficiencies.

Grading and Assessment

The five-point grading system is used in Germany’s Masters Programs and courses. Here, the passing grade may range between 1.0 (or the best) and 4.0 (or narrow pass). Let’s look into the details –
4.0 and 5.0-grade bands are used to mark the failing work when the work doesn’t reach up to the required standards. The final grade is determined by summing up the complete performance of the students across all the modules and dissertation. The calculation is performed with each component weighted as per the ECTS credit level.
Funding and Fee

Public and private universities of Germany are considered as a better academic option as they charge a minimum fee. The Masters in Germany is available for students across the
globe and it offers a fair education to German, EU, and non-EU students. Some exceptions and criteria are mentioned here –
  • Private universities charge a fee, although the other German higher education systems are publically funded.
  • The state of Baden-Wuerttemberg charges €1,500 per semester to international (non-EU) students.
  • Some courses are designed for experienced professionals. A few non-consecutive Master courses charge fees.

Application process

It is hard for postgraduate applications to find a centralized portal. Students are expected to find a course of their interest and then apply to their respective universities. A few universities have opted for Uni-Assist to manage the applications, coming across the globe.
No rigid deadline system is applied to the universities. Each one is free to make and apply an own deadline criterion that needs to be applied at least four months in advance (especially if it seeks time to organize a student visa).
The students can create simultaneous applications by keeping enough time to manage and complete them well.
Though it is an individual decision, universities may charge the processing fee from the students that can hardly go up to €50. 
Uni-Assist service differs in terms of performance and fees that ultimately reflects on the additional assistance.

Admissions requirements 

A suitable Bachelors's degree is the key requirement for admission into a Masters's in Germany. The Bachelor's degree should be recognized by the German universities. The students are not compelled to get a Bachelors's degree from only Germany University. 
Uni-Assist helps the students for getting admission into a German University.
EU’s ENIC –NARIC academic recognition centers can also assist the students in the entire admission process.

If any additional entry requirement exists, students can check for some other requirements that may happen in the restricted places –
  • Secondary educational details: Some German universities may seek additional details from the international students to know more about their educational history. You may consider it as a ‘school-leaving certificate’ that is equivalent to the German Hochschulzugangsberechtigung. British GCSEs or A-levels (or their equivalents) like certificates are also fine.
  • Interview: If a German university wants to discuss more your experience and application, video interviews may take place.
  • Entry tests: Standardized postgraduate admission tests or any other additional entry exam may take place for the competition as well as specialized programs. These tests for business school and MBA programs can also require the score from the recognized tests like GRE or GMAT.
  • The above-mentioned details are a complete representation of the requirements that German universities may seek. Not everything is going to be asked or expected. The courses or university can also get satisfied with even a recognized Bachelors's degree.

Language requirements

Since students are coming across the globe, various German Master's degrees are taught in English for better understanding. The students may need to provide a language test score to study in Germany to assure the language. Your course will decide the further path –
  • Programs in English: Though it doesn’t seek a proficiency in German, the non-native English speakers need to pass the test to continue the studies. Here, if the students have completed an undergraduate degree course (or a similar one) in the English language, things can vary.
  • Programs in German: These programs need to be done by the international applicants who want to attend the courses in the German language. These students should verify their capability in qualification. Now, the score decides whether the student is allowed to take admission in a particular university or not. Some universities can give an exemption to clarify and take further German language training before they commence the degree.

It is always worth to take a German language test whether it is required by the university or not. This is the ultimate opportunity to build up additional language skills by studying abroad. If you are getting additional/parallel course training, it is like an advantage to the international students.
This additional learning and test will help you in making a better relationship with Germany. You can gain the skills and proficiency to add to your resume that will ultimately put additional weight on your performance.

Numerous clauses (the restricted application)

Numerus clausus translates as ‘restricted number’. A few German master programs are subject to this term i.e. numerus clausus. This, somehow, indicates the total number of students that the program can admit.
In this way, Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmacy fields are much affected.
Here, we are listing the two major types of numerus clausus that German Universities usually apply –
  • The centrally restricted (by the German government) subjects are known as zentraler numerus clausus.
  • The locally restricted (by universities themselves) subjects are known as lokaler numerus clausus.

This is the University’s task to clarifying the things well in front of every student that which numerus clausus they are applying. The discussion should be made before processing the application.

Application through Uni-Assist

Some German universities have Uni-Assist Internation application portal.
Don’t forget to check the specifically required Masters Program that you need. University may only use Uni-Assist for the specific ones.
Uni-Assist may differ in its performance with different universities and programs. You need to be sure whether they are valid or not. The foreign qualification and transcription need to be understood through recognition and accreditation.
While completing the application, Uni-Assist either forwards the application to the university or generates a VPD (Vorpruefungsdokumentation). This further helps the students in completing the application.
The current set fees of Uni-Assist is €75 where €15 can be added further as the additional university charge within the same semester. Students can use the Uni-Assist service s for multiple applications without incurring any prohibitive cost.
The good news is that some universities can even pay these Uni-Assist fees for you that is further known as ‘cost transfer’.

Student Visa

Every year, several students move towards Germany for their career development. The international students are receiving a warm welcome from the land. The country opens borders with relaxed and effortless immigration agreements with various European countries (Schengen Area).
Visa requirements
Here are a few details that you must know regarding German student visa, immigration, and residence (on the basis of individual nationality) –
  • The EU, EEA, or Swiss students don’t need a visa for studying Masters Courses in Germany. Still, students need to have a residence permit.
  • Apart from the above-mentioned places, students from other countries need a normal visa and residence permit, both.
A tourist visa is not applicable for your studies in Germany, though you can convert this visa into a student applicant visa or student visa. This Visa also helps the students for their short courses if they want to pursue language training like programs.

  • Global Ranked Institutions: Germany owned many renowned universities and institutions. The place has eight Global Ranked Institutions that are featured in the top 100 institutes.
  • Dedicated Research Institutes: There are dedicated research centers in Germany that adding more expertise to the universities here. The prestigious Max Planck Institute is one of them.
  • Affordability: The most important thing that sets the German universities away from the universities of the UK and the USA is their affordability. Many German universities have zero requirements as their tuition fee for Ph.D. students (irrespective of their nationality).
  • The Ph.D. origin: The modern thesis-based research degree program i.e. Ph.D. is basically developed in Germany.

German Universities and Types

With more than 500 higher education institutions, Germany has gained much popularity among the students. These universities are generating highly trained researchers. The German Higher Education System includes several types –
  • Research Universities (Universität): These universities are responsible for carrying the academic researches on different subjects.
  • Technical Universities (Technische Universität): These universities are specialized in technology, engineering, and science related researches. 
  • Universities of Applied Science (Fachhochschulen): This focuses on vocational and professional subjects like business, engineering, or social science. They basically don’t award the PhDs to the students.
  • Research Institutes: They carry important research projects in partnership with industry, businesses, and universities. They also operate within the larger networks like the Max Planck Society.
  • Colleges of Art, Film, and Music: This focuses on the practical and performance-related tasks. It also doesn’t provide PhDs to the students.

Public and Private Universities

Research or technical universities and institutes are giving a great opportunity to Ph.D. students. There are 16 states (lander) in Germany where each one is responsible for administering their public universities. They also provide them with funding. Some other public universities are also getting the funds from the Catholic or Protestant church. Around 95% of other students within the country are studying in 400 Germany Public Universities for their Ph.D. course. 
The rest 5% of the students are attending the 120 private universities. These private universities don’t receive state-level funding and most of this doesn’t offer Ph.D. programs.

Ph.D. Structure

As per the European qualification framework and Bologna Process, a doctorate in Germany is a third-cycle qualification. German PhDs are, somehow, following the format of the Bologna Process. But they are still a bit different in nature as it doesn’t take it completely as the third phase of studies. It further considered PhDs as a separate and higher research achievement.

Types of PhDs in Germany

There is a need for independent research towards the submission. A doctoral degree is all about the examination of a thesis. This was a German innovation, which is still available at many universities here. Apart from that, some other universities also offer more ‘structured’ programs:
  • Traditional Ph.D.: The traditional Ph.D. is the one where a student identifies the research project and starts on it independently under an expert supervisor (Doktorvater / Doktomutter). Students can choose the desired institution where they want to conduct the research, either in a German company or organization. 
  • Structured Doctoral Programs: The Structured Doctoral Programs are largely conducted in English. The programs are internationally-oriented and it lets the students complete the other training along with their thesis. They also include collaboration and placements with the other external research institutes.

The Length of Program

There are usually two semesters in one academic year in Germany. The starting and completion date may vary in accordance with the institute and course structure. The two semesters are mentioned here –
  • The Wintersemester (WiSe): From 1st October to 31st March (two-week break at Christmas and Easter).
  • The Sommersemester (SoSe): From 1st April to 30th September (a break from July to September).
The complete length of a Ph.D. depends upon your selection of the program. Either it is a traditional Ph.D. or structured doctoral program; it takes around 4 and 3 years respectively.

The German Ph.D. process

This again depends upon your selection of the type of doctorate program. Traditional and structured doctoral programs are involving a research project and a thesis requirement. Apart from this, the key differences between both are mentioned here –
  • Traditional PhDs: These PhDs award more flexible and independent Ph.D. There is no such compulsion for attendance, curriculum, and deadlines. All you need is to complete the research thesis and that is it. 
  • Structured Doctoral Programs: These programs include compulsory seminars, lectures, and interim assessments. The transferrable skills training in academic or scientific methods and soft skills are also available. The students work on major research projects, either individually or collaboratively. 
However, the majority of students prefer traditional doctorate. On the other hand, there is a constant growth in the number of people who choose structured doctoral programs, especially in the mathematics and natural science realm.

Assessment and Examination 

Since there are two types of doctoral programs, the assessment and examination procedure also differ in those terms. Both are discussed here, separately –
The traditional Ph.D. requires the submission of a doctoral thesis. The student further needs to complete an oral presentation and examination of work, which is further known as Rigosorum. The presentation and all are performed in front of the relevant professors of the specific field. When the oral examinations are replaced with a defense of the thesis, it is known as Disputation. The thesis defense is more focused on the conducted research. On the other hand, an oral examination is highly focused on the level of knowledge you have.
Structured programs are giving the typical requirements for the doctoral students where they need to attain around 180-240 ECTS credits. Students need to complete several compulsory units. With all the seminars and lectures, your knowledge and comprehension will be noticed. You will need to submit a thesis and complete the oral examinations in a bit more advanced manner.

Fees and Funding

Doctoral degrees in Germany are normally free for all national and international students. It is a generous public investment in education. The students may require some amount as the other parts of fees during their complete study.

Ph.D. fees

In Germany, the doctoral level of education and tuition is free for the students, irrespective of the nationality of the students. The students may need to pay the tuition fee for the extended period of their education if they continue, which is apart from the standard length of a regular Ph.D. i.e. three years or six semesters.
Although there is no such fee to be charged from the students, some of approx €250 is required as a semester contribution i. e. Semesterbeitrag. This amount covers many expenses like administration costs, student governance, and service (Studentenwerk).

Living costs

Living cost is generally higher in Germany in comparison to other European countries. Since you are not paying tuition fees, your only and key expense is the living cost within Germany. German Studentenwerk (student union network) international projects that a student may need to have around €850 for the required expenses like food, accommodation, and other needs. 
The term accommodation itself offers three different options to the international students within Germany:

  • Hall of residence: A student needs to spend around €160-360 per month for a single dormitory room. This may further include health insurance and a Semesterticket for transport.
  • Wohngemeinschaften: This is basically private shared flats. WG is very popular and the cheapest accommodation in Germany that costs around €150-350 per month.
  • Private rental: This is the most expensive accommodation option that costs around €500 per month.

Scholarships

Germany offers various scholarship programs to international Ph.D. students. This further allows them to cover different expenses and living costs while studying –

  • Student Grant: Supervisor may nominate you for a grant of around €1,250 per month from the German National Academic Foundation (Studienstiftung des Deutsche Volkes).
  • Deutscher Akademischer Austausch Dienst scholarships: Deutscher Akademischer Austausch Dienst (abbreviated DAAD) is a scholarship of €1,200 per month, offered by the German Academic Exchange Service. These scholarships are given to foreign students for their Ph.D. in Germany.
  • StipendiumPlus: This scholarship is offered by a group of 13 organizations. International students in Germany are enjoying funding of around €1,350 per month.
The different funding programs are designed in Germany for soothing the life of international students. In the structured doctoral degree program of Ph.D., the students will receive a monthly allowance of around €1,000 to €1,400 along with their studies.

Work along with studies

Germany offers great working opportunities to the students along with their studies. They can earn side by side without any compulsion of nationality –

  • The students from the EU, EEA, and Switzerland can work along with their studies. They don’t need any residence permit and if they are working over 20 hours in a week, the students can pay national insurance contributions as well without any restrictions on hours.
  • Apart from the above-mentioned nationalities, other students are having a restriction on working hours as they can work for either 120 full-days or 240 half-days per year. If students want to exceed the working days, they need to take permission from the local employment agency i.e. Agentur für Arbeit, and Foreigner’s Registration Office i.e. Ausländerbehörde.
International Ph.D. students are getting a great working opportunity as student assistance and teaching appointments. You can also supervise the library, research literature for professors, and demonstrate in labs. The salary will be applied according to the work that doesn’t rely on the 120-day rule.

Ph.D. application in Germany

Germany has a different application procedure than many other countries across the globe.
For Traditional PhDs, students need to find a supervisor. You will request the supervisor to supervise your thesis in your program.
For Structured PhDs, the applications are directly made to the institution (or graduate school) for the required program.

Entry requirements

Prior to the doctorate, a student must complete the academic study of a minimum of eight semesters. This will make you compatible or equivalent to a German Master's degree that will let you continue for the doctorate programs.
Your qualification should be recognized by Dekanat i.e. Dean’s Office or Promotionsausschuss i.e. Board of Examiners of the university you are applying for.
On the flip side, a fast-track program also exists for exceptionally well-qualified international students. They can take admission onto a Ph.D. program and all they need to do is to complete an entrance examination.

Language requirements

The language requirement is such a crucial thing if you are willing to start a Ph.D. in Germany. But it basically depends upon your course selection. 
In Traditional PhDs, students need to write a thesis in German. Some also allow their students to write in other languages. You may need to prove German language proficiency to represent your knowledge in this language by getting certified through DSH or TestDaF.
In Structured doctoral programs, students are taught in the English language. If a student coming from a nation where English is the first language, the rules are different. Other than this, the students need to complete an English language proficiency test like IELTS or TOEFL. Institutions are free to set their thresholds for students.

Application procedure

Here are the normal application requirements for a Ph.D. in Germany that a student normally require –

  • In traditional Ph.D. projects, students need to have a statement from his or her doctoral supervisor. The statement should be submitted by describing the intention of projects.
  • Students should submit various academic documents. The certified copies of academic transcripts from the previous degrees need to be submitted before starting the program.
  • Students need to submit proof of recognition, especially for the qualification from the Dean’s Office or University Board of Examiners.
  • Academic references are also required where you need to include at least two professors as referees with whom you have worked.
Students need to submit the above-mentioned requirements to the relevant department / doctoral committee. This will further confirm your eligibility to begin a Ph.D. program.

Interviews

Some institutions may include an interview as an essential step for admission into Structured Ph.D. programs. The interview will be performed in front of the supervising board for the program. On the other hand, traditional Ph.D. programs need an interview that can be conducted with the chosen supervisor. This interview seems more informal than the previous one. Skype interviews are the most preferred way for international students.

Student Visa

Since Germany is one of the most popular destinations for international studies among the students, it has kept an easy immigration system for international students. Students can freely enter Germany and start their studies without any requirement of a Visa.

Visa requirement

Though Germany has no such Visa requirement for the students from various other locations, some other details should be discussed here. The students from the following countries need no visa for their studies in Germany –
  • The EU, EEA, and Switzerland
  • Australia, Israel, Canada, USA, Japan, South Korea, and New Zealand
  • Students must hold a Special Administrative Region passport if they belong to China, Hong Kong, and Macao
  • Students must have an identity card number on the passport if they belong to Taiwan.
  • Students must hold a biometric passport if they belong to Albania, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Georgia, Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, and Ukraine
  • Students must not intend to seek separate employment before or after degree if they belong to Andorra, Brazil, El Salvador, Honduras, Monaco, and San Marino

If you belong to any country, other than the above-mentioned locations, you must obtain a visa as an international student. You will need to enter into the Visa requirement to start the Ph.D. program in Germany.

Visa Types

Two types of Visa are required for Ph.D. students in Germany –

  • VisumzurStudienbewerbung is a Student Applicant Visa that allows the students to enter Germany for three months to complete the admission. You can use this to opt for a full student visa.
  • VisumzuStudienzwecken is a Student Visa that allows the students to enter Germany for up to three months once accepted for PhD study. Hereafter, you can apply for a residence permit.
Irrespective of the Visa requirements, students will be required to register the presence in Germany when they enter –

  • Bürgeramt / Bürgerbüro is the Resident Registration Office where the international students (all nationalities) need to register themselves within a week of arrival in Germany. Students will receive a Meldebestätigung as the confirmation of their registration to allow their stay in Germany.
  • Ausländerbehörde is the Alien Registration Office in Germany where the Non-EU/EEA students will apply for a residence permit before their visa expires.

The requirements for Visa

Students need to go through a few requirements for their Visa or residence permit. Here are the required documents –
  1. Academic documents are required along with a letter of admission to a recognized German university. Full academic transcripts are required.
  2. Personal documents include a passport along with two passport photos, which are valid for the duration of PhD. This further includes a tenancy agreement as proof of a secured accommodation.
  3. Other documents are also required in terms of health insurance (for overall stay), language qualifications (for the language of thesis), and evidence of financial resources that costs around €10,332 per year. If you are also applying for a residence permit, Meldebestätigung is also required. This residence permit and Visa will cost €110 and €75, respectively. 

Health insurance

Every resident in Germany should have valid health insurance that abides by the laws. Otherwise, you can’t apply for a Visa or get enrolled at any university.
European Health Insurance Card (abbreviated EHIC) is here for the students from the EU. Germany has some social insurance agreements with the European Union member states to cover many required things.
Many insurers exist in Germany, which is offering medical insurance to international students. Some universities also provide advice and assistance with their relevant international office.

Next steps

Germany paves the way for a prosperous career. It becomes necessary, to begin with, an apparent career planning during the doctorate. You can also start learning in Germany, preferably.

After Ph.D. work opportunity in Germany 

After Ph.D., the working regulations depend upon the nationality of the individual students.
If you belong to the EU and EEA countries, you don’t need any work permit after your Ph.D. You will be offered the same access to employment opportunities as the German nationals have.
If you belong to any country, other than the EU and EEA, you may need to extend the residence permit for up to 18-months.

EU Blue Card

After getting a job in Germany, you will need to apply for a German residence permit or an EU Blue Card. EU Blue Card is required if you want to work in any other EU state that again requires a settled job of at least €49,600 per year.

title: City Registration
body:
City Registration for Foreign Students in Germany: A Complete Guide

When moving to Germany for studies or work, one of the first things foreign students need to do is register their address with the local authorities. This process, known as "Anmeldung", is mandatory and serves as a cornerstone for accessing various services in Germany. In this guide, we’ll walk you through everything you need to know about city registration.

What is Anmeldung?

Anmeldung is the process of registering your residence in Germany. Every person living in Germany—including foreign students—is required by law to register their address within two weeks of moving into their new accommodation. This registration applies whether you live in a student dormitory, shared flat (WG), or private apartment.

Failure to register your address can lead to fines and complications with essential services like opening a bank account, getting health insurance, or obtaining a residence permit.

Why is Anmeldung Important?

Anmeldung is more than just a bureaucratic formality. It is crucial because:

  1. Residence Proof: You will need your registration certificate ("Meldebescheinigung") to:

    • Open a bank account.

    • Enroll in health insurance.

    • Apply for a residence permit.

    • Sign contracts, such as for internet or phone services.

  2. Tax ID Number: During Anmeldung, the tax office ("Finanzamt") generates your tax ID number ("Steueridentifikationsnummer"), which you’ll need if you start a job.

  3. University Enrollment: Some universities may ask for proof of Anmeldung as part of their enrollment process.

Steps for City Registration

Follow these steps to complete your Anmeldung process smoothly:

1. Prepare the Necessary Documents

Before visiting the registration office, ensure you have the following documents:

  • Completed Anmeldung Form: You can download this form from the website of your local "Bürgeramt" (registration office) or get it in person.

  • Passport or National ID: Bring your valid identification document.

  • Rental Agreement ("Mietvertrag"): This proves you have a place to live.

  • Landlord’s Confirmation ("Wohnungsgeberbestätigung"): A signed document from your landlord confirming you’ve moved in.

2. Find Your Local Bürgeramt

Search for the Bürgeramt office closest to your residence. Larger cities may have multiple offices, and you can typically book an appointment online.

3. Book an Appointment

In busy cities like Berlin or Munich, appointments may be booked weeks in advance. It’s advisable to schedule your appointment as soon as possible after moving in. In smaller towns, you might be able to register as a walk-in.

4. Visit the Bürgeramt

On the day of your appointment, arrive on time with all the required documents. After submitting your documents, the officer will process your registration and provide you with your Meldebescheinigung (registration certificate).

5. Keep the Meldebescheinigung Safe

Your Meldebescheinigung is a key document that you will need for various administrative tasks. Keep both physical and digital copies for your records.

Common Challenges and Tips

  1. Language Barrier: Many forms and interactions at the Bürgeramt are in German. Consider bringing a German-speaking friend or using translation apps.

  2. Appointment Delays: In major cities, appointments can be hard to get. If your two-week deadline is approaching, you can often register without an appointment by explaining your urgency.

  3. Landlord Cooperation: Ensure your landlord provides the "Wohnungsgeberbestätigung" on time, as it is a mandatory document.

  4. Updates Needed for Moves: If you move to a new residence within Germany, you must repeat the Anmeldung process for the new address.

Exemptions and Special Cases

  • Short Stays: If you plan to stay in Germany for less than three months, you generally don’t need to register.

  • Temporary Housing: For temporary accommodations like hotels, you might need to register once you move to a permanent address.

FAQs

1. What happens if I don’t register?

Failure to register can result in fines up to several hundred euros and complications with accessing essential services.

2. Can I register without a permanent address?

No, you need a valid address and the landlord’s confirmation to complete the Anmeldung.

3. Do I need to de-register when leaving Germany?

Yes, before leaving Germany permanently, you must de-register ("Abmeldung") at your local Bürgeramt.

Conclusion

Completing the Anmeldung process is a vital first step for foreign students arriving in Germany. By registering your address promptly and keeping your Meldebescheinigung safe, you’ll set yourself up for a smooth transition into life in Germany. If you’re planning your move, prepare in advance to make this process stress-free.

title: Tax ID
body:
Tax ID (Steueridentifikationsnummer) for Foreign Students in Germany: A Comprehensive Guide

When moving to Germany for work or study, understanding the importance of the Tax ID, or Steueridentifikationsnummer, is crucial. This unique identification number is necessary for anyone earning income in Germany, including foreign students. This guide will help you navigate the process of obtaining and using your Tax ID.

What is a Tax ID?

The Steueridentifikationsnummer (commonly referred to as Tax ID) is an 11-digit unique number assigned to every resident in Germany for life. It is used by the tax authorities to identify individuals for tax purposes. Unlike a Tax Number (Steuernummer), which is specific to freelancers or businesses, the Tax ID applies to all residents, including students.

Why Do You Need a Tax ID?

A Tax ID is essential for:

  1. Starting a Job: Employers require your Tax ID to calculate and deduct income tax correctly.

  2. Opening a Bank Account: Some banks may ask for your Tax ID during the account opening process.

  3. Filing Tax Returns: If you’re eligible for a tax refund, your Tax ID is mandatory for filing your return.

  4. Receiving Scholarships or Financial Aid: Institutions may require your Tax ID for disbursements.

How to Obtain a Tax ID

Your Tax ID is automatically issued when you register your address (Anmeldung) in Germany. Here’s how it works:

1. Automatic Issuance Through Anmeldung

  • Step 1: Complete your city registration (Anmeldung) at the local Bürgeramt. You’ll need documents such as a valid passport, rental agreement, and landlord’s confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung).

  • Step 2: After Anmeldung, your details are forwarded to the Finanzamt (tax office).

  • Step 3: Within 2-3 weeks, your Tax ID will be mailed to your registered address.

2. Requesting a Tax ID from the Finanzamt

If you haven’t received your Tax ID or need it urgently:

  • Visit your local Finanzamt office.

  • Bring your Anmeldung certificate (Meldebescheinigung) and passport.

  • Request your Tax ID in person. In most cases, they can provide it immediately or send it by post.

Using Your Tax ID

Your Tax ID is used in various financial and administrative tasks. Common scenarios include:

  • Providing to Employers: Share your Tax ID with your employer during onboarding.

  • Filing Annual Taxes: Use your Tax ID when submitting tax declarations.

  • Applying for Benefits: Some social benefits or government programs require your Tax ID.

Lost Your Tax ID?

If you lose your Tax ID, don’t worry. You can retrieve it by:

  1. Contacting the Finanzamt: Provide your personal details, and they can reissue the Tax ID.

  2. Checking Old Documents: Your Tax ID might be listed on previous tax returns or official correspondence.

  3. Using the Online Portal: Some Finanzamt offices offer online retrieval services for registered users.

FAQs

1. Do I need a Tax ID if I don’t have a job?

Yes, even if you don’t have a job, you might need your Tax ID for tasks like opening a bank account or applying for financial aid.

2. How long does it take to get a Tax ID?

It typically takes 2-3 weeks after Anmeldung. If you need it sooner, you can visit the Finanzamt directly.

3. Is the Tax ID valid for life?

Yes, your Tax ID is valid for life and does not change, even if you move within Germany.

Conclusion

The Tax ID is a fundamental part of settling into life in Germany. Whether you’re starting a job, opening a bank account, or filing taxes, having your Tax ID ready ensures a smooth process. Make sure to keep it safe and accessible, as you’ll need it repeatedly.

title: Social Insurance
body:
Social Insurance (Sozialversicherung) for Foreign Students in Germany: What You Need to Know

Germany’s social insurance system is an integral part of its welfare state, providing essential protections to residents, including foreign students. If you plan to study or work in Germany, understanding the Sozialversicherung system is crucial. This guide breaks down what social insurance entails, its benefits, and how foreign students can navigate it.

What is Social Insurance?

Social insurance (Sozialversicherung) in Germany is a mandatory system that provides financial and health protections for residents. The system covers various aspects of life, ensuring support during sickness, old age, unemployment, and accidents.

As a foreign student, you may be required to contribute to certain social insurance schemes, especially if you work while studying.

Why is Social Insurance Important?

Social insurance ensures:

  1. Access to Healthcare: Health insurance is compulsory and provides access to Germany’s high-quality medical services.

  2. Financial Security: Contributions to pension and unemployment insurance protect you in the long term.

  3. Legal Compliance: Enrolling in social insurance is mandatory for anyone working in Germany.

Components of Social Insurance

Germany’s social insurance system comprises five key components:

1. Health Insurance (Krankenversicherung)

Health insurance is compulsory for all residents. Foreign students can choose between:

  • Public Health Insurance (Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung): Affordable and widely accepted.

  • Private Health Insurance (Private Krankenversicherung): Offers tailored plans but may have higher premiums.

2. Pension Insurance (Rentenversicherung)

Even as a student, if you’re working and earning above a certain threshold, contributions to pension insurance are mandatory. These contributions accumulate and can benefit you in retirement.

3. Unemployment Insurance (Arbeitslosenversicherung)

Unemployment insurance provides financial support if you lose your job. Students typically contribute if they work more than 20 hours per week or hold certain types of employment contracts.

4. Accident Insurance (Unfallversicherung)

Accident insurance covers medical expenses and rehabilitation costs in case of workplace accidents. This is usually paid by employers, so students don’t contribute directly.

5. Long-Term Care Insurance (Pflegeversicherung)

This insurance supports individuals who need long-term care due to illness or disability. Contributions are mandatory and deducted alongside health insurance.

How to Register for Social Insurance

1. Obtaining a Social Security Number (Sozialversicherungsnummer)

  • Step 1: Your employer or health insurance provider will usually register you for social insurance and request your Sozialversicherungsnummer.

  • Step 2: The German Pension Insurance (Deutsche Rentenversicherung) will issue your number.

  • Step 3: Keep this number safe, as it is required for all employment and social insurance matters.

2. Enrolling Through Employment

If you start a job in Germany, your employer will automatically enroll you in the necessary social insurance schemes. Ensure you:

  • Provide your health insurance details.

  • Confirm deductions on your payslip for social insurance contributions.

Costs and Contributions

Social insurance contributions are shared between employees and employers. As a student:

  • Health Insurance: Approximately 7.3% of your gross salary.

  • Pension Insurance: Around 9.3% of your gross salary.

  • Unemployment and Long-Term Care Insurance: Additional deductions apply if your earnings exceed specific thresholds.

Exemptions and Special Cases

  • Mini-Jobs (450-Euro Jobs): Students with mini-jobs are exempt from most social insurance contributions, except for pension insurance (which can be waived).

  • Scholarship Holders: If your income is solely from scholarships, you are not required to contribute.

  • EU Students: Those with an EHIC card may be exempt from German health insurance but must verify coverage.

FAQs

1. Do I need social insurance if I don’t work?

Health insurance is mandatory regardless of employment. Other components depend on your job status.

2. Can I choose my health insurance provider?

Yes, you can select from public or private health insurers based on your needs and eligibility.

3. What happens if I don’t register for social insurance?

Failure to register can result in fines and loss of access to essential services.

Conclusion

Social insurance is a cornerstone of Germany’s welfare system, offering protection and support for residents. As a foreign student, understanding and complying with these requirements ensures a smooth and secure stay in Germany. Take the time to register, contribute, and enjoy the benefits of this robust system.

title: Criminal Record Certificate
body:
Criminal Record Certificate (Führungszeugnis) in Germany: A Guide for Foreign Students

If you are planning to study or work in Germany, you might be asked to provide a Criminal Record Certificate (Führungszeugnis). This document verifies whether an individual has a criminal history and is often required for job applications, visa processes, or university admissions. Here is everything you need to know about obtaining this certificate as a foreign student in Germany.

What is a Criminal Record Certificate?

The Führungszeugnis is an official document issued by the Federal Office of Justice in Germany. It provides a summary of a person’s criminal history, or the lack thereof. Employers, universities, and government agencies may request this certificate to verify an applicant’s legal background.

Why Do You Need a Criminal Record Certificate?

A Criminal Record Certificate may be required for:

  1. Job Applications: Employers, especially in sensitive sectors like education or healthcare, often require this certificate.

  2. Visa Applications: Some visa categories mandate a clean criminal record.

  3. University Enrollments: Certain courses or internships may request this document.

  4. Volunteering: Organizations working with vulnerable populations may ask for an enhanced certificate.

Types of Criminal Record Certificates

There are two main types of Führungszeugnis in Germany:

1. Standard Certificate

This version is for general purposes, such as job applications or visa requirements. It contains a basic summary of criminal convictions.

2. Enhanced Certificate

Required for positions involving work with children or vulnerable groups, this version includes additional details to ensure suitability for such roles.

How to Apply for a Criminal Record Certificate in Germany

Application Process

  1. Visit the Local Bürgeramt: Applications can be submitted at the local registration office (Bürgeramt).

  2. Submit the Application Form: Fill out the form requesting a Führungszeugnis.

  3. Provide Identification: Present a valid passport or residence permit.

  4. Pay the Fee: The standard fee is approximately €13.

  5. Receive the Certificate: The document is typically sent to your registered address or directly to the requesting institution.

Required Documents

  • Valid passport or national ID.

  • Proof of registration (Meldebescheinigung) from the local registration office.

  • Any official letter or form specifying the type of certificate required.

Criminal Record Certificates from Your Home Country

If you are a new arrival in Germany, you may also be asked to provide a criminal record certificate from your home country. The process varies by country but usually involves:

  1. Applying through your local police department or a government agency.

  2. Getting the document authenticated or apostilled if required.

  3. Translating the certificate into German by a certified translator.

Processing Time and Fees

  • Processing Time: It usually takes 1-2 weeks for the certificate to be issued.

  • Fees: The standard fee is €13 for most applications. Enhanced certificates may incur additional charges.

FAQs

1. Can I apply for a Criminal Record Certificate online?

Yes, applications can also be submitted online via the Federal Office of Justice’s portal if you have a registered eID (electronic ID).

2. Do students always need a Criminal Record Certificate?

Not necessarily. It depends on the specific requirements of the job, university, or visa application.

3. What if I have a criminal record?

Minor offenses may not impact your application, but serious crimes could lead to visa or job application denials.

Conclusion

Obtaining a Criminal Record Certificate is a straightforward process but essential for various applications in Germany. Whether you need it for employment, education, or legal purposes, understanding the requirements and procedure ensures a smooth experience.

title: Ausbildung
body:
An Ausbildung is a paid apprenticeship that ends in a nationally recognised qualification. You spend part of each week at a company and part at a vocational school, and you are an employee from the first day — not a student paying fees.

Length
2 to 3.5 years
You are paid
From month one, rising yearly
German needed
B1 at least, usually B2
Tuition
None

Why people choose it over a degree

A degree teaches a subject; an Ausbildung teaches a trade, and it does so inside a real company. You finish with three or four years of employment history, a qualification employers recognise everywhere in Germany, and no debt. For many trades it is the normal route — German employers do not treat it as a lesser path, and it is often the faster one into stable work.

The trade-off is commitment. You choose a field at the start and the training is specific to it. Changing direction later is perfectly possible, but it means starting something new rather than adjusting a general degree.

How the dual system works

"Dual" means two places of learning, running side by side throughout.

  • The company — typically three or four days a week. Real work, supervised, with responsibility that grows as you do.
  • The Berufsschule — one or two days a week, or in blocks of several weeks. The theory behind the trade, plus general subjects.

Your training runs on a contract with the company, and the curriculum is set nationally. An Ausbildung in one city therefore means the same thing as the same Ausbildung in another.

Getting a place

  1. Choose the trade first

    There are over 300 recognised occupations. Narrowing that down is the real work, and it is worth doing properly before you write a single application.

  2. Get your German to the level the employer wants

    This is where most applications fail. You will work with colleagues and customers in German and sit school exams in German. B2 makes you a credible candidate; B1 is the floor, and only for some trades.

  3. Apply to companies, not to schools

    The company selects you, and the school place follows from the contract. Applications usually open around a year before the late-summer start.

  4. Sign the Ausbildungsvertrag

    The training contract sets out the trade, the length, your hours and your pay. Nothing else can happen until you have one.

  5. Apply for the visa, if you need one

    Non-EU applicants apply for a vocational training visa on the strength of the signed contract. Expect the embassy to test your German and to want proof you can support yourself.

What you are paid

Trainees receive a monthly training allowance that increases with each year of training. There is a statutory minimum, and many sectors pay well above it under collective agreements. It is a real wage rather than a token — enough to live on modestly in most cities, though tight in Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

Training pay is revised most years and varies by trade and region. Check the current rate for your specific occupation before you build a budget around a number.

At the end

You sit a final examination set by the relevant chamber — the IHK for commercial and industrial trades, the HWK for craft trades. Pass it and you hold a qualification recognised nationwide and understood by every employer in the field.

Many trainees are kept on by the company that trained them, which is the outcome the system is built to produce. If you are not, or you would rather move, non-EU graduates of the system can get a residence permit to look for related work.

Where German fits in

Almost all of this runs in German: the application, the interview, the working day, the school, and the final exam. Reaching B2 before you apply is not a formality to clear — it is what decides whether the rest is possible at all.

title: Praktikum
body:
A Praktikum is an internship. Whether yours must be paid, and whether it uses up your permitted working days, turns on a single distinction: is it required by your course, or did you choose it?

Two kinds
Required, or voluntary
Typical length
Two to six months
Pay
Depends which kind
German needed
B1 to B2 for most

The distinction that decides everything

Settle this before you accept anything.

Pflichtpraktikum — required by your course

Your study regulations demand it. It is part of the qualification, and your university will confirm that in writing.

  • Exempt from the minimum wage, so it may pay little or nothing.
  • For non-EU students, it does not use up your annual working days.
  • No separate permission is needed from the immigration office.

Freiwilliges Praktikum — voluntary

You arranged it because it is useful, not because the course requires it.

  • If it runs longer than three months, the minimum wage generally applies.
  • For non-EU students, it does count against your annual working days.
  • Worth clearing with the immigration office before you start a long one.

The pay rules have exceptions — short placements and orientation placements before a course among them. If an employer says the minimum wage does not apply, ask which exception they are relying on.

Finding one

  1. Start six months out

    Larger companies recruit interns on the same timetable as graduates. Smaller firms move faster but advertise less, so approaching them directly works.

  2. Write a German application

    A one-page Anschreiben and a tabular Lebenslauf. German CVs are factual and plain — no personal statement, no design flourishes.

  3. Get the paperwork right before you sign

    If it is a Pflichtpraktikum, have your university's written confirmation in hand. That document is what determines your pay and your working-day position.

  4. Read the contract

    It should state the dates, the hours, the pay and what you will actually be doing. A placement that cannot describe your tasks is unlikely to teach you much.

What it is worth

A German internship is the most reliable way into a German employer. It gives you references from people who have watched you work, vocabulary no classroom provides, and an honest sense of whether the field suits you. A great many permanent jobs in Germany go to former interns.

The language part

Some international firms run in English, and their internships are open to you with less German. Most do not. B1 is enough to be useful in a patient team; B2 is what lets you take part properly — in meetings, on the phone, and in the corridor conversations where the real learning happens.
