title: Finding somewhere to live
body:
Housing is the hardest part of arriving in Germany, and it blocks everything else — you cannot register your address, and therefore cannot open a bank account or complete your enrolment, until you have somewhere to live.

Start looking
Three months ahead
Deposit
Up to three months' rent
You will need
A landlord's confirmation
Hardest cities
Munich, Frankfurt, Hamburg

The document that matters most

When you move in, your landlord must give you a Wohnungsgeberbestätigung — a signed confirmation that you live there. Without it you cannot register your address, and without registration almost nothing else in Germany works.

Ask for it on the day you get the keys. A landlord is obliged to provide it, and one who hesitates is a warning sign.

Three kinds of home

Studentenwohnheim — student halls

Run by the local Studentenwerk. By far the cheapest option, and the waiting lists reflect that. Apply the moment you have an offer of a place, not when you arrive.

WG — a shared flat

The usual choice, and the most sociable. You take one room in a flat and share the kitchen and bathroom. Existing tenants pick their new flatmate, so expect something closer to an interview than an application. It is also the fastest way to improve your German.

Your own apartment

The most private and the most difficult. Landlords typically want proof of income, a credit report and references — hard to supply when you have just arrived and have no German credit history.

Understanding the rent

Two numbers appear in every advertisement, and the difference between them is substantial.

TermWhat it means
Kaltmiete"Cold rent" — the rent alone, nothing included.
NebenkostenService charges: heating, water, rubbish, building upkeep.
WarmmieteCold rent plus service charges. This is what you actually pay each month.
KautionThe deposit. Capped by law at three months' cold rent, returned when you leave.

Compare listings on the Warmmiete. A low Kaltmiete with high Nebenkosten can cost more than it first appears. Note too that electricity is usually not in the Nebenkosten — you arrange that separately.

How to search

  1. Begin three months before you move

    In the big cities, earlier. Halls in particular have waiting lists measured in semesters.

  2. Prepare your documents as one file

    Passport, proof of enrolment or your job contract, proof of income or a guarantor, and a credit report if you have one. Rooms go to whoever replies first with everything attached.

  3. Write a short, specific message

    Who you are, what you do, when you would move in, how long you intend to stay. Two paragraphs. In German if you can manage it — it visibly helps.

  4. View before you commit

    In person, or by video call with someone you can see. Never transfer money for a place you have not viewed.

  5. Get the confirmation on moving day

    The Wohnungsgeberbestätigung, signed. Then register your address within two weeks.

Avoiding the scam

Housing scams target new arrivals, and they follow a pattern worth knowing: an unusually cheap flat, an owner conveniently abroad, a story about keys being posted, and pressure to send a deposit today to secure it.

No genuine landlord in Germany needs money before you have seen the property and signed a contract. If you are asked to pay first, walk away — it is a scam every time.

If nothing comes through in time

Take temporary accommodation and keep searching from inside the country. A hostel, a sublet or a short-term rental for a few weeks is far better than accepting something unseen. Many people arrive on a temporary arrangement and find their real home within a month, once they can view places in person.

title: Electricity
body:
Electricity is usually the one utility you arrange yourself. It is not normally part of your service charges, and if you do nothing you will be supplied anyway — on the most expensive tariff available.

Who arranges it
You, not the landlord
Do it
Within two weeks of moving
You need
Your meter number and reading
Switching
Free, and worth doing

The default that costs you money

Every address has a basic supplier — the Grundversorger — who must supply anyone who asks. Move in without arranging anything and you are automatically their customer. The power works, the bills arrive, nothing is wrong.

It is simply the most expensive tariff on the market. The default exists to guarantee supply, not to be good value. Switching to a normal contract is straightforward and usually saves a meaningful amount over a year.

Setting it up

  1. Read the meter on the day you move in

    Photograph it, with the meter number visible. This is the single most useful thing you can do, and it takes a minute. It is what stops you being billed for the previous tenant's use.

  2. Compare tariffs

    Comparison sites are the normal route. Look past the headline price at the contract length, the notice period, and whether the first-year discount disappears afterwards.

  3. Sign up with your chosen supplier

    You give the address, the meter number and the opening reading. If you are switching, the new supplier handles the cancellation — you do not contact the old one.

  4. Set the monthly payment sensibly

    You pay a fixed amount each month called the Abschlag, estimated from expected use. Set it too low and you face a large bill at the annual reconciliation.

How the billing works

German electricity billing is an estimate that gets corrected once a year, which surprises people who expect to pay for what they used each month.

You pay the same Abschlag every month. Once a year the meter is read properly and the supplier compares real use against what you paid. Use less than estimated and you get a refund; use more and you owe the difference in one payment. Keep a little aside for that.

The broadcasting fee

Separate from electricity, but it arrives at the same time and confuses almost every new arrival. The Rundfunkbeitrag funds public broadcasting and is charged per household, not per person. It is mandatory whether or not you own a television.

One flat pays once. In a shared flat, one person registers and the others contribute — you do not each pay. If a letter arrives demanding it, do not ignore it; if a flatmate already pays, you simply say so.

Energy prices and the broadcasting fee both change from time to time. Treat any figure you read online as indicative and check the current one before budgeting.

When you move out

Read the meter again on your last day, photograph it, and give your supplier notice with a forwarding address. Skip this and the final bill follows you — sometimes for months, and sometimes to the wrong address.

title: Heating and water
body:
Unlike electricity, heating and water are usually handled by your landlord and paid through your monthly service charges. You do not sign a contract — but you do get an annual statement, and it can go either way.

Who arranges it
Your landlord, normally
You pay via
Monthly Nebenkosten
Settled
Once a year
Watch for
Damp and mould

How you pay for it

Heating and water sit inside the Nebenkosten, the service charges bundled into your monthly rent. You pay an estimated amount each month along with the rent itself.

Once a year your landlord produces a Betriebskostenabrechnung — an itemised statement setting real costs against what you paid. If you used less than estimated, you are refunded. If you used more, you pay the difference as a single sum.

German law requires most heating costs to be billed by actual consumption rather than split evenly, which is why flats have individual heat meters or radiator devices. Turning your heating down genuinely reduces your bill.

Reading the annual statement

It is worth actually reading. Statements contain mistakes, and you have a limited window to query one.

  • Check the meter readings against your own, if you noted them.
  • Check that the period covered is right, particularly in your first year.
  • Check that costs are split by a sensible measure — floor area or consumption, not by nothing in particular.
  • Only certain costs may be passed on. Repairs and management fees generally may not.

If a statement looks wrong, say so in writing promptly. There is a deadline for objecting, and a statement left unchallenged is treated as accepted.

Heating a German flat

Radiator valves are numbered rather than marked in degrees. The numbers set a target temperature, not a rate of heating — turning a cold room to 5 does not warm it faster, it simply overheats it and costs more.

SettingRoughlySuits
112 °CAway for a few days
216 °CBedroom, overnight
320 °CLiving room, comfortable
424 °CWarmer than most people need
528 °CRarely sensible

Never let a room drop below about 15 °C in winter, even an unused one. Cold walls attract condensation, and condensation causes mould.

Mould, and why it becomes your problem

German flats are well sealed, which keeps heat in and moisture in with it. Cooking, showering and drying laundry indoors all release water into the air, and with nowhere to go it condenses on the coldest surface in the room.

The expected remedy is Stoßlüften: open windows fully for five to ten minutes, two or three times a day, and close them again. Brief and complete beats a window left permanently ajar, which cools the walls without clearing the air.

This matters beyond comfort. If mould appears and the landlord can show you did not air the flat properly, the cost of putting it right can fall to you. Airing daily in winter is not fussiness — it is how these buildings are meant to be lived in.

When something breaks

Heating failures are the landlord's responsibility. Report them in writing, keep a copy, and give a reasonable deadline. If heating is out for a prolonged period in winter you may be entitled to reduce your rent — but tell the landlord first and put it in writing, rather than simply paying less.

title: Professional jobs
body:
Germany has a shortage of qualified people and has rewritten its immigration law to attract them. If you hold a recognised qualification, the route in is more open than it has been for decades — but it runs through two gates: recognition of your qualification, and language.

First step
Get your qualification recognised
German usually
B2, sometimes B1
Regulated fields
Recognition is compulsory
Job-seeking visas
Available to qualified applicants

Recognition comes first

A German employer needs to know what your qualification means. Anerkennung is the formal process of comparing it against the German equivalent, and it decides whether you may work in your field at all.

Regulated professions

Medicine, nursing, law, teaching, and much of engineering. You cannot practise without recognition — no exception, no employer workaround. Start this before anything else, because it is slow.

Everything else

Recognition is not legally required, but it makes you far easier to hire, because it turns an unfamiliar credential into one the employer understands. For most fields it is worth doing.

Recognition takes months and needs certified translations of your certificates and transcripts. Begin while you are still in your home country, where the original documents are easier to obtain.

Routes in

  1. A job offer first

    The cleanest route. With a qualification and a contract above the relevant salary level you can apply for a work permit, and for graduates in shortage fields the thresholds are lower.

  2. Come to look for work

    Germany offers residence permits that let qualified people enter and job-hunt from inside the country, which is considerably more effective than applying from abroad. Conditions and names change — check the current rules with the German mission where you live.

  3. Convert from study

    If you graduate from a German university you may stay on to look for work related to your degree. This is the smoothest path of all, and one reason studying here is worth considering.

How much German you need

More than job advertisements imply. A posting in English often describes a team that works in German once the meeting ends.

LevelWhat it opens
B1Some international companies and IT roles. Daily life is manageable.
B2The realistic working standard. Most employers ask for this, and most regulated professions require it.
C1Client-facing work, medicine, law, teaching, management.

B2 is the level that changes what is available to you. Below it you compete for a small pool of English-speaking roles; at it, you compete for the actual job market.

Applying, German style

German applications are formal and consistent, and departing from the convention reads as carelessness rather than personality.

  • Anschreiben — a one-page letter, addressed to a named person, explaining why this role and this company.
  • Lebenslauf — a factual tabular CV, reverse-chronological, typically two pages.
  • Zeugnisse — certificates and references, attached as scans. Germans expect these with the application, not later.

Photographs on a CV are no longer required and are increasingly left off. Include one only if you want to.

A realistic sequence

Start recognition, and study German while it is being processed. Those two run in parallel and both take months, so beginning them together saves the better part of a year. Apply once you have recognition in hand and B2 behind you — that is the point at which German employers can actually say yes.

title: Student jobs
body:
Studying in Germany comes with the right to work, but that right is limited and the limits are counted precisely. Exceed them and you risk your residence permit, so it is worth understanding them properly before you take a job.

Non-EU limit
Days per year, counted
Term time
Around 20 hours a week
Semester breaks
Full time is possible
Studies
Must stay your main activity

What you are allowed

EU and EEA students

The same rights as German students. No permit, no day limit. Work as much as your course allows — though above roughly twenty hours a week during term you begin paying full social contributions.

Non-EU students

You may work a fixed number of full days per year, or twice as many half days, without asking anyone's permission. The allowance was increased in recent years, so older guides understate it — and it is exactly the sort of figure that changes, so confirm the current number with your immigration office rather than trusting any website, including this one.

Two things matter more than the number itself:

  • Keep a record. Days are counted across the year and across every employer. Nobody tracks them for you, and you may be asked.
  • Work at your university does not usually count. Research and teaching assistant posts are generally outside the limit, which makes them worth seeking out.

Working beyond your allowance is a breach of your residence permit, with consequences reaching as far as losing it. If you are near the limit, stop and ask the immigration office.

The Werkstudent job

A Werkstudent role is part-time work in your field of study, alongside your course, and it is the most valuable kind of student job in Germany.

  • Around twenty hours a week during term, full time in the breaks.
  • Paid noticeably better than casual work.
  • A special rule exempts working students from most social insurance contributions, so more of the wage reaches you.
  • It is genuine experience in your field, and it is how a great many graduates get their first permanent job.

Non-EU students should note that the day limit still applies. A Werkstudent contract does not remove it.

Tax and insurance, briefly

Earn very little and you will pay almost nothing. Cross certain monthly thresholds and income tax and social contributions begin, and the amounts are recalculated when you file a return — students who overpay usually get it back.

You need a tax identification number, which arrives automatically after you register your address. Give it to your employer or you will be taxed at the highest rate until you do.

Health insurance is compulsory throughout, and student rates are heavily reduced. Working more can change your insurance position, so tell your insurer if your hours rise substantially.

Finding work

  1. Look at your own university first

    Assistant posts, library and lab work, and department jobs. Well paid, sympathetic to your timetable, and often outside the day limit.

  2. Then look in your field

    A Werkstudent role related to your degree is worth several times a casual job — for the pay, and much more for what it does to your CV.

  3. Use German where you can

    Hospitality, retail and delivery work is available with modest German, but the better-paid and more interesting jobs need B1 or B2. Language is what moves you from one category to the other.

  4. Keep your own log

    A simple record of days worked, by employer. Ten minutes a month, and it settles any question about your allowance instantly.

Keeping the balance right

Your permit exists so that you can study; work is permitted alongside it, not instead of it. Students who take on too much lose semesters, and a delayed degree costs far more than the extra shifts earned. Treat the limit as a sensible ceiling rather than a target.

title: Other kinds of work
body:
Not all work in Germany is a normal contract. Mini-jobs, freelancing and volunteering each follow their own rules on tax, insurance and — if you are not an EU citizen — whether you are allowed to do them at all.

Minijob
Low monthly earnings, low deductions
Midijob
The band just above
Freelance
Needs permission on most permits
Volunteering
Unpaid, and genuinely so

The Minijob

A Minijob is employment below a set monthly earnings threshold. It is the most common form of casual work in Germany and the simplest to hold.

  • The employer handles a flat-rate contribution; you take home almost all of the wage.
  • You keep whatever health insurance you already have.
  • You may opt out of pension contributions, though staying in is often worthwhile.
  • All the usual employment rights apply — paid holiday and sick pay included, which surprises people.

The threshold is tied to the minimum wage and therefore moves most years. Exceed it regularly and the job stops being a Minijob, with different deductions from that point.

Earnings thresholds change annually. Ask your employer to confirm the current limit in writing rather than working from a figure you found online.

The band above it

Earn more than the Minijob threshold but still modestly, and you land in a transitional band — sometimes called a Midijob — where social contributions phase in gradually rather than all at once. It exists so that a small pay rise cannot leave you worse off. There is nothing to apply for; payroll handles it.

Freelancing and self-employment

This is where people get into trouble without realising, and it is worth being blunt about.

A student residence permit generally allows employment within your limits. It does not automatically allow self-employment or freelance work. Taking on freelance clients without permission can breach your permit even if the work is small and occasional.

  1. Ask the immigration office first

    Permission is often granted, and asking costs nothing. Proceeding without it can cost a great deal.

  2. Register with the tax office

    Self-employment means registering, charging VAT once you pass a turnover threshold, and filing an annual return.

  3. Sort out your insurance

    Self-employed income can change your health insurance status and cost. Tell your insurer before you start, not afterwards.

Volunteering

Unpaid work for a charity, a community group or a cultural organisation. It does not count as employment and does not touch your working-day allowance, provided it is genuinely unpaid — a small expenses allowance is fine, a wage in disguise is not.

It is an underrated way to practise German. You are surrounded by native speakers doing something concrete together, which teaches you more in a month than the same time spent reading.

Work to be careful of

Undeclared cash work exists and is offered to new arrivals. It leaves you with no insurance if you are injured, no recourse if you are not paid, and a serious immigration problem if it is discovered. The saving is never worth it.

Be wary too of any "job" that asks you to pay upfront, to receive and forward money, or to use your own bank account for someone else's payments. The last of these is money laundering, whatever it is called in the advert, and the criminal liability lands on the account holder.

Where German makes the difference

Casual work is available with very little German, and it pays accordingly. The gap between a warehouse shift and an office Minijob is largely a language gap — B1 opens most casual work, and B2 opens the kind that looks like a career later on.

title: Before you start the placement test
body:
This test is here to find the level you are actually at, so we can put you in the right class. It is not an exam you can pass or fail, and there is no advantage in scoring higher than your real level.

Why this matters. A score that flatters you puts you in a class where you cannot follow, and you lose weeks. A score that reflects you puts you where you will learn. Nobody sees this result but us.

What we ask of you

  1. Work alone

    No help from anybody — not a friend, not a family member, not a teacher. If someone is sitting with you, ask them to leave you to it.

  2. No dictionary, no translator, no AI

    No dictionary in print or online, no Google Translate or DeepL, no ChatGPT or any other AI assistant, no browser translation, no grammar checker. Close the other tabs.

  3. No searching, no notes

    Do not look anything up while the test is open, and do not use notes, textbooks or previous answers.

  4. Give yourself enough time

    Sit somewhere quiet where you will not be interrupted, and do the whole test in one go. Rushing it produces a level that is not yours.

  5. Write properly in the writing task

    The written answer should be at least 8 to 14 sentences. A one-line answer tells us nothing, and we cannot place you on it.

  6. Leave it blank rather than guess wildly

    If you genuinely do not know, that is useful information. A lucky guess is not.

What we do with the result

  • We use it to recommend a level and a course. That is all.
  • It is not a certificate and carries no weight outside LangNation.
  • It is not shared with anyone outside the school.
  • Your teacher may look at it, so they know where you are starting from.

If the level turns out wrong

It sometimes does — a test is a snapshot. Tell your teacher in the first week and we will move you, at no cost. That is much easier than discovering it in week six.

Honesty

We cannot watch you take this test, and we are not going to try. We are asking you to be straight with us because it is your time and your money at stake.

If a placement turns out to be far from what the test suggested, we will simply retest you in class and place you where you actually are.

title: Teacher Terms and Conditions
body:
These terms govern your work as a teacher for LangNation and your use of the teacher portal at langnation.com/teach. Please read them before setting up your account — you are asked to accept them when you do.

Plain summary. Everything the school gives you to teach with — course materials, lesson plans, recordings, student lists — stays LangNation's property. You may use it to teach LangNation students, and for nothing else. You may not sell it, publish it, pass it to another school, or use it in private lessons of your own. When you stop teaching for us you return or delete all of it, along with anything holding student data.

You are free to teach elsewhere. What you are not free to do is take our materials with you.

This summary is for orientation only; the numbered clauses below are what apply.

§ 1 Scope

These terms apply between LangNation ("the school", "we", "us") and you as a teacher, whether you are employed by us or engaged as a freelancer. They sit alongside your individual contract of employment or engagement. Where that contract says something different, it takes precedence over these terms.

The provider is the company named in our Imprint.

§ 2 Your teacher account

An account for the teacher portal is created by the school and claimed by you through a one-time link sent to your email address. There is no public sign-up: the account gives access to the personal data of real students, and who receives one is a decision the school makes.

  • Your account is personal. Never share your password, and never let anybody else use your account — not a colleague, not a family member, not a student.
  • Tell us immediately if you believe somebody else has your password or has used your account. We can end every session on it at once.
  • You are responsible for what happens under your account until you tell us.
  • We may suspend an account at any time, and will do so as a precaution if we believe it has been compromised.

§ 3 Student data and confidentiality

Through the portal you can see the names, email addresses, telephone numbers and course records of the students in your classes. This is personal data, and it belongs to the students, not to us and not to you. We hold it as controller under the GDPR; you handle it on our instructions.

You may use student contact details for teaching your own classes — arranging a lesson, sending a worksheet, following up an absence.

You may not, whether during or after your engagement:

  • use student details to advertise your own lessons or anybody else's;
  • copy class lists, export them, or keep your own separate record of students beyond what teaching requires;
  • pass any student's details to a third party, including another school, a tutoring agency or a recruiter;
  • add students to mailing lists, messaging groups or social platforms unconnected with their course;
  • discuss an identifiable student's progress, circumstances or payments with anybody outside the school.

This duty of confidentiality continues after you stop teaching for us, without limit of time.

If you become aware of any loss, unauthorised disclosure or accidental deletion of student data — a lost laptop, a message sent to the wrong person, a shared link left open — you must tell us without delay and in any event within 24 hours. The law gives us 72 hours to report certain incidents to the supervisory authority, and that clock starts when the incident happens, not when we hear about it.

§ 4 Teaching materials — ownership

All course materials, lesson plans, scripts, slide decks, worksheets, audio and video recordings, mock examinations, question banks, curricula, templates and internal documents made available to you by the school remain the property of LangNation or of their respective authors. Nothing in your engagement, and nothing in being given access to them, transfers ownership or copyright to you.

Where you create teaching materials as part of your work for the school, and the school has paid for that work or commissioned it, the rights to use those materials belong to the school, to the extent permitted by law and by your individual contract. You keep the right to be named as their author. If you bring materials of your own that you created before and independently of your work for us, they stay yours; tell us in writing what they are, so that neither side is later mistaken about it.

§ 5 Teaching materials — what you may and may not do with them

What you may do. You receive a simple, non-exclusive, non-transferable right to use the school's materials for one purpose: teaching LangNation students. That includes preparing your lessons, presenting the materials in class, and giving them to the students enrolled on the course you teach.

What you may not do. You may not, whether for payment or free of charge:

  • sell, licence, rent out or otherwise commercialise the materials;
  • use them in private lessons of your own, or in teaching for any other school, agency, platform or employer;
  • give them to anybody who is not a LangNation student or a LangNation colleague — including former students after their course has ended, except for the copies they already properly received;
  • publish them, upload them to any website, file-sharing service, public cloud drive, messaging group or social platform;
  • use them to create a derivative course, book or video of your own;
  • remove or alter any notice of authorship or ownership.

To be clear about the boundary: you are free to teach privately, and free to work for another school. Nothing here prevents that. What this clause prevents is doing it with our materials, which we paid to make and which are the reason a LangNation course is worth what it costs.

A breach entitles us to end your engagement without notice and to pursue the remedies copyright law provides. Where materials have been passed beyond the permitted circle, we may require you to recover or delete them and to tell us where they went.

§ 6 When you leave

When your engagement ends, for any reason, you must within fourteen days:

  • return every physical item belonging to the school — printed materials, books, equipment, keys, access cards;
  • delete every digital copy of the school's materials from your own devices, personal cloud storage, email archives and messaging apps, including copies in drafts, downloads and recycle bins;
  • delete every copy of any list, export or note containing student data;
  • hand over the current version of any materials you produced for the school, in an editable format;
  • leave any shared drive, group chat or class channel belonging to the school;
  • confirm to us in writing that you have done all of the above.

Your portal account is closed at the same time, and every session on it ends. You may ask us for a copy of your own personal data at any point; that right is separate and is unaffected by this clause.

Nothing in this clause requires you to delete anything you are legally obliged to keep, or anything that is genuinely your own under § 4.

§ 7 Lessons

  • Be ready at the scheduled time, with a working device, a stable connection and a headset.
  • Open the class room yourself and stay until the lesson ends.
  • If you cannot teach a lesson, tell the office as early as you can so that a substitute can be arranged. Tell the office, not the class.
  • Keep the class list, attendance and any marks up to date in the portal.
  • Treat every student courteously and equally, whatever their background, nationality, religion, gender or ability.

Do not record, photograph or stream a lesson without the express consent of everybody taking part, and never publish a recording. Recordings made for the school are the school's material and fall under §§ 4 to 6.

§ 8 Fees and invoicing

Your rate, working hours and payment intervals are those set out in your individual contract of employment or engagement, not in these terms.

Where you are engaged as a freelancer you are responsible for your own tax and social security, you decide how you carry out the work, and nothing in these terms is intended to create an employment relationship. Where you are employed, your contract of employment governs and takes precedence.

§ 9 Liability

We are liable without limitation for injury to life, body or health caused by our negligence, and for damage caused intentionally or by gross negligence. For slight negligence we are liable only where an obligation is breached whose fulfilment makes proper performance possible at all and on which you may reasonably rely, and then only for damage typical of this kind of contract and foreseeable when it was made.

Where you are employed, the established principles of limited employee liability for work-related activity apply in your favour, and nothing here reduces them.

§ 10 Data protection

We process your own personal data — your name, contact details, the classes you teach and the times you signed in — to run the school and to meet our legal obligations. What we collect, why, how long we keep it and what rights you have are set out in our Privacy Policy.

Records that the law requires us to keep, such as those needed for tax or employment law, are kept for as long as the law requires and no longer.

§ 11 Changes to these terms

We may amend these terms where there is a valid reason, for example a change in the law or in how the school works. We will tell you at least six weeks before a change takes effect. If you do not object in writing before then, it is treated as accepted; we will say so expressly in the notice.

Where a change would materially worsen your position and you object, either side may end the engagement at the point the change would take effect, subject to the notice period in your individual contract.

§ 12 Final provisions

German law applies. Where you are an employee, the mandatory protections of employment law apply whatever this says.

Should any provision be or become invalid, the remainder stays in force.

Version: these terms apply from the date shown on this page. The version you accepted when you set up your account is recorded against it, and is the one that applies to you until you are notified of a change.

title: Delete Your LangNation School Account

At LangNation School, we respect your privacy and provide a way to request deletion of your account and associated personal data.

  2. Use the email address associated with your LangNation School account.
  3. Our support team will verify your request and process the deletion.

What Data Will Be Deleted?

Following verification, we will delete or anonymize applicable account information, including:

  • Personal profile information
  • Account login information
  • Learning progress and vocabulary records
  • Homework submissions and associated learning data

Certain records may be retained where required by law or for legitimate purposes, such as accounting obligations. We will inform you about any applicable retention.

Contact Us

For questions about account deletion or privacy, contact:

Email: info@langnation.com

Website: https://langnation.com
